d.title: The first matching clause wins, and the name is gone after the block
d.caption: **Clauses are tried top to bottom and the first match wins — so a broad clause above a narrow one makes the narrow one dead code**, and nothing warns you. The second half is the part that bites: **`as err` is deleted at the end of the `except` block, so reading `err` afterwards raises `NameError`.** Python does that deliberately, **to break the reference cycle between the exception and the frame that caught it** — which means anything you still need must be copied out inside the block.

d.title: The handler claimed a failure from the success path and logged the wrong cause
d.caption: **Anything inside `try` is protected — so if the success path raises the *same* exception class you are catching, your handler claims it and reports the wrong cause.** The measured output is exactly that: **`unknown user: u_1` for a user who exists, because `user["email"]` raised `KeyError` inside the `try` and the handler blamed the lookup.** And the log line is **confidently wrong, which is worse than silence.** Moving the send to `else` makes the real traceback appear: **`KeyError: 'email'`, pointing at the line that actually failed.**

steps.code: send inside the try, missing user
send inside the try, user exists

d.title: A `return` in `finally` drops the exception that was in flight
d.caption: **`finally` runs no matter how control leaves the `try` — and if control leaves the `finally` by a different route, that new route *replaces* the old one.** So the first row returns `-1` and the exception simply disappears: **no traceback, no log, a function that reports failure as a value nobody checked.** The same applies to `break` and `continue` in a loop. And the last row is the correct behaviour for comparison: **an inner `finally` that does not redirect control lets `boom` reach the outer handler.**

d.title: Five needs, and `try/finally` is the right answer to exactly one of them
d.caption: **For a resource you acquired, `with` puts the guarantee with the resource rather than in every call site** — so `try/finally` survives only for **things with no context manager: a raw handle, a temporary global, a monkeypatch in a test.** The others each have a named tool: **`suppress` is narrow, self-documenting and impossible to widen by accident; `ExitStack` unwinds a runtime-determined number in reverse order; and `@contextmanager` with a `yield` inside `try/except/else` puts a commit-or-rollback policy in one place.**

state: the guarantee lives with the resource

d.title: Four forms, and two of them damage the traceback
d.caption: **`raise NewError(...) from err` joins the two with “The above exception was the direct cause”; a bare `raise` inside `except` re-raises untouched; and `raise NewError(...)` without `from` still chains, with the weaker “During handling of the above exception” phrase.** The form to avoid is `raise err`: **it re-raises the same object but appends the current frame, so the traceback now shows the `except` block as well as the real origin** — and in a deeply nested call chain that buries the line you needed.

state: appends this frame - buries the origin

d.title: Eleven fields in one line, and five of them you added
d.caption: **A structured line is a JSON object rather than a sentence, which is what makes it queryable: `order_id`, `customer_id` and `request_id` are fields you can filter and group by**, not substrings you have to parse out of prose. Five come from the logging framework (**timestamp, level, logger, module, line**), one from `logger.exception` (**the full traceback, as a field**), and the rest are the ones you passed. And the format is the whole argument: **“error processing order 8821” cannot be grouped by customer; this can.**

state: group by, and join to data

d.title: Passing a request id through every signature is the obvious approach and it is unbearable
d.caption: **In a service handling concurrent requests, interleaved log lines are useless without something tying one request's lines together** — and the obvious fix, threading a `request_id` parameter through every function, touches every signature in the call chain including the ones that do not log. **A filter reading a `ContextVar` does it in one place**: the entry point sets the variable, the filter attaches it to every record, and **no intermediate function knows the id exists.** And `ContextVar` rather than a thread-local **because it follows an `await` across tasks.**

d.title: One `dictConfig` call, and one default that silences everything
d.caption: **`disable_existing_loggers: False` is essential — the default `True` silences every logger created before the call, which includes all of them if configuration happens after imports.** The deployment answer is shorter than people expect: **in a container, log to stdout and stop thinking about it** — files inside a container die with it, rotation fights the orchestrator, and the platform already collects stdout. And if you must ship from inside the process: **wrap the handler in `QueueHandler` with a `QueueListener`, so the emitting thread never blocks on the network.**

nodes.label: dictConfig: the whole setup in one place
In a container: log to stdout
Files inside a container die with it

d.title: Two failure modes, and each has a characteristic way of being got wrong
d.caption: **The division is about what continuing would produce: wrong data means fail fast, a smaller but correct result means degrade.** The trap rows are the useful part. **Being defensive about your own bugs hides them** — a `try/except` around a calculation that should never fail converts a loud bug into a quiet wrong number. And **degrading something that was never optional makes a partial result look complete**, which is the worse of the two because nothing downstream can tell.

d.title: Fourteen commands, and four of them are the ones people never find
d.caption: **`until N` escapes a loop without stepping every iteration**, which is the command that makes `pdb` usable on a loop at all. **`a` prints the current function's arguments and is the right first command after landing in a frame.** **`display x` shows a value after every step when it changes**, replacing a dozen repeated `p x`. And **`interact` opens a full REPL in the frame**, for anything a single expression cannot express. The rest is navigation — **and `ll` first, always.**

d.title: The bug diagnosed in four commands, after the crash, with no re-run
d.caption: **The most useful `pdb` feature is the one people never find: you can inspect a crash *after* it happened, with the entire stack and every local still intact** — no re-running and no guessing what the values were. The session is the whole argument: **`bt` locates the frame, `a` shows `quantity='2'` as a string, `p type(...)` confirms it, and `u` plus one more read finds the source: `'legacy-import'`.** Four commands from traceback to root cause, **and the information was all sitting in a process that had already stopped.**

d.title: Six symptoms, and the highest-value move is the least technical
d.caption: **Logging the inputs and replaying locally turns an unreproducible bug into a reproducible one, which is the highest-value move on the list** — everything else only narrows where to look. Two tools are worth knowing by name before you need them: **`py-spy dump --pid` gives the stack of a live process without stopping it or importing anything into it**, which is the only option on a hung container, and **`faulthandler.enable()` produces a Python traceback from a fatal signal, which otherwise prints nothing at all.**
